teaching: There is no permanent one (mustaqarr) besides Ali; he is the one in whose gnosis the intellects of the wise are bewildered, he has no peer, and he is wise in his actions.
The Imam-e-Mustaqarr (Permanent Imam) is Maulana Ali, the son of Janab Abu Talib, who is the appointed successor.
For every Natiq (Speaking Prophet) there is always a Wasi (legatee), and from the progeny of the Wasi the Imamat continues unbroken.
Ali is both the Wasi of the Prophet (Wasi-e-Paighambar) and the Imam-e-Mustaqarr simultaneously.
The Prophet received what he received because of Ali's trustworthiness; the amanat (trust) was for Ali, and the Prophet was called Amin and Sadiq because Ali delivered that trust.
In his capacity as Wasi, Ali is of a lower rank than the Prophet, but his Muhtajib (veiled essence) is the 'Ayn-e-'Azima (Essence of Grandeur).
The Prophet's name in the heavens was Ahmad, while Muhammad is the name given on earth.
The verse 'Wa in tawallaw fa inna Allaha 'alimun bi'l-mufsidin' is read as: if they deny the wilayat of Ali, Allah is well aware of the conspiracies of those mischief-makers.

The verse 'come to a word equitable between us' (kalimatin sawa') esoterically commands the kalimah-reciting Muslims to accept the wilayat and obedience of Ali, whose being is the word of justice and fairness.
Regarding the station of Ali one must neither commit ghuluw (exaggeration) nor fall short, must associate no partner in his station, and must make no one from among oneself an Imam.
If the enemy does not accept the Wasi, the follower of the Wasi must distance himself and declare disassociation (barat) from them.
In the Dar-us-Satr (Period of Concealment) there is a command to keep the batin (inner reality) hidden through taqiyyah until the Imam's command is received.
Printing and distributing books of haqaiq (esoteric realities) without the Imam's permission is wrong, even if done with good Arabic and intentions.

When Hazrat Asif Fyzee wished to print the Da'im ul-Islam he was denied permission until he received the command of his elder, Sayyidna Taher Saifuddin; he printed it without that permission, which was wrong.
One must act upon the command of the subordinate authority (the Da'i, the Mansub) placed below the Imam.
The verse 'why do you argue about Ibrahim while the Tawrat and Injil were revealed only after him' rebukes the People of the Scripture, since Ibrahim preceded both Judaism and Christianity.

Within every one of the 124,000 prophets there is a distinction between mustaqarr (permanent) and mustawda' (temporary), per the principle 'fad-dalna ba'dahum 'ala ba'd' (We preferred some over others).
Ibrahim held the rank of khullat (close friendship) and per 'wa ja'alna Ibrahim imama' was made an Imam, raising the question of whether he was an Imam or a Prophet.
The Ibrahim cast into the fire in the Quran was not Ibrahim Khalilullah but a Da'i who served as the Hijab (veil) of the Imam; all du'at are in the veils of the Imam.

Da'ud Qutub was designated a mustawda' and not a mustaqarr; he was not made the owner (malik), and he wrote khatam bosi (a token of subservience) at the bottom of his letters because he was a junior to the appointed head.
Sayyidna Jalal received the nass (designation) only 13 days before his death and within those days completed all the necessary appointments and demotions among the du'at.
The great fitna (schism) arose at the time of Sayyidna Sulayman, when Da'ud bin 'Ajab Shah throughout his life disputed Sulayman's rank.
Ibrahim is a Mustaqarr Imam, the son of Janab Salih, whose lineage has continued from the beginning.

The chain of the Mustaqarr Imam passes from father to son 'wahidan 'an wahidin' (one after another), an extended rope (Habl-ul-Mamdud) that is never broken and persists from one kawr (cycle) to another across all dawr, kawr, athar, and adwar.
The succession of father-to-son in the Imamat is a sunnah of Allah, not a sunnah of the Prophet, and per 'wa lan tajida li-sunnatillahi tabdila' it can never be changed.
The son of a Da'i does not necessarily become a Da'i (he becomes one only if capable), but the son of an Imam must become the Imam; this is the specific principle of the da'wah.
After Ibrahim the Matter of Imamate (Amr-e-Imamat) was divided into two parts: Imamat-e-Mustaqarr (Permanent Imamate) and Imamat-e-Mustawda' (Deputized Imamate).
The opponents claimed that Muhammad was merely sent (mab'uth) to renew the shari'at of Ibrahim and was a mustawda' with no share in the Permanent Imamate, a claim the discourse refutes.
The Permanent Imams (A'imma-e-Mustaqarrin) appointed the Deputized Imams (Mustawda'in) only after the death of Ibrahim, and every mustaqarr appoints a mustawda' for his service by his own command.
Maulana Ibrahim appeared at a special juncture when 3000 years had passed for the world.
Ibrahim's two sons were Isma'il, whose rank was very high as an Imam-e-Mustaqarr, and Ishaq, who held the rank of a prophet but was a mustawda'.

Isma'il was told to take future service from the progeny of Ishaq, and Ishaq and his progeny were bound to obey Isma'il; this arrangement continued for 3000 years in Lebanon, Syria, and the Middle East.
The reward for the sincere service of Ishaq's progeny to the Imam of every age was granted at the time of the Prophet, and the Prophet's reward was the fruit of that service.
The prophets Ayyub, Yusuf, and Ya'qub, from the progeny of Ishaq, served the Imams (Faizar, Nawat, Salam and others) who succeeded Isma'il, by the command of the Imam.
Just as the Prophet worked by the command of the Imam, in the present era the du'at work by the command of the Imam.
After a thousand years of the Prophet the era changed into the era of the Qa'im, at which time the ranks of the du'at were elevated.
The opponents wanted the Prophet to grant them a portion of the rank of istida' (being a deputy), but this was not the Prophet's job.
Esoterically a shay' (thing) means a believer, nisf-e-shay' (half a thing) means a hypocrite, and la-shay' (nothing) means a disbeliever, related to the Urdu lasha (a soulless corpse).
The opponents have no gnosis (ma'rifat) of Ali the Wasi, so arguing and debating about him yields no result.

The verse 'Ma kana Ibrahim yahudiyyan' means Ibrahim was neither excessive nor deficient: he was a sincere hanif Muslim, no polytheist, who gave every rightful person his due equally and gave his appointed successor everything in entirety.
The din (religion) of God is one from Adam onward, but the shari'at (law) has kept changing, Adam's shari'at differing from Nuh's and others.
The era of sitr (concealment) is always divided according to the Nutqa (Speaking Prophets): the eras of Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa are named, but never the era of Isma'il, Hasan, or Husayn.

Yaqub al-Sijistani holds that six shari'ats passed (Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa, and the Prophet), of which three are fathers (aba': Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim) and three are sons (abna': Musa, 'Isa, the Prophet).
In reality there were only three shari'ats, and the latter three came to expand and renew them: Musa expanded Adam's shari'at, 'Isa expanded Nuh's, and the Prophet expanded Ibrahim's.
Many rulings in the present din come from the shari'at of Ibrahim, such as zabihat (ritual slaughter) and khatna (circumcision), because Ibrahim Khalilullah is among the Prophet's ancestors.

The verse 'Inna awla an-nasi bi-Ibrahim' means the people closest to Ibrahim are the Guiding Imams (A'imma-e-Hadin) whose chain of Imam-after-Imam remains, not the prophets whose ranks (Lut, Ishaq, Isma'il) are separate.

Isma'il's rank is very lofty as an Imam-e-Mustaqarr, while Ishaq is a mustawda' (a caretaker who acts as commanded), and Lut's rank is intermediate between Ishaq and Isma'il with attributes neither of them had.

The verse 'Ma kana li basharin' means no human prophet given the Scripture, authority, and prophethood would ever tell people to be his servants rather than Allah's, but would say be rabbaniyyin (people of the Lord).

No Mustawda' has the right, when the Imam al-Zaman entrusts him with the rank of Natiqiyyat, authority in the Da'wat, and wondrous sciences, to then tell his murids that he himself is the Imam al-Mustaqarr.
The Mustawda' must instead tell his Hudud al-Da'wat to keep clarifying the great rank of the Imam al-Zaman to the people, so that they make no one else their Lord (Rabb).
No Mustawda' has the right to rise to the level of the Mustaqarr; the Imam al-Zaman is the master (malik) who alone entrusts the Natiqiyyat.
The 'human' (bashar) referenced in the verse is the Mustawda', and Mustawda'in of lower rank must not consider themselves to have become the Imam al-Mustaqarr.

The da'wat is always given toward the Imam al-Zaman, never toward the speaker himself; the support (ta'id) flows from the Imam, and every speaker must confess that he is only the medium and says nothing of his own.

The verse 'Wa la ya'murakum an tattakhidhu al-mala'ikata wan-nabiyyina arbaba' means a true prophet would not command you to take the angels and prophets as lords, nor command disbelief after submission.
He cannot tell you to take the Hudud al-Da'wat and the Mustawda'in as Lords besides the Imam al-Mustaqarr, for the same revelation that guides cannot then misguide.
The verse 'Wa idh akhadhallahu mithaqan-nabiyyina' records Allah taking the covenant of the prophets that they must believe in and support the messenger who confirms what is with them.
The Sabiq-i-Ta'ala took a covenant from the Mustawda'in to remain steadfast on the gnosis (ma'rifat) of Amir al-Mu'minin and to immediately accept the confirming messenger when he comes.

Sabit qadam (steadfastness) means being saved from both ghuluww (exaggeration, ghayn=1000) and quluww (falling short, qaf=100); the midpoint 500 is the letter seen, signifying firm obedience to Allah, the Messenger, the Imam, and the hudud.

The verse 'Qala a'aqrartum wa akhadhtum 'ala dhalikum isri' records Allah taking the prophets' acknowledgment of the burden and making them witnesses, esoterically the acknowledgment of the station of the Wasi.
Wherever Allah is mentioned in the covenant verses, the Wasi is being mentioned, and the mustajibin-e-da'wat (respondents of the mission) are made witnesses to the covenant.
The verse 'Faman tawalla ba'da dhalika fa'ula'ika humul-fasiqun' means whoever turns away after the covenant exits the religion and becomes a fasiq.
Breaking the covenant ('ahd) reaches the stage of disbelief (kufr) and makes one deserving of Hell.
The breakers of the covenant (Nakithin-e-'ahd) were the Jews in one era, and among us the Sunni and Shia sects are the Nakithin, Mariqin, and Fasiqin.
The Nas'aluka-llah prayer distinguishes the believers from the Daudis (who do not have it) and seeks refuge from the three: Mariqin, Nakithin, and Fasiqin.

The verse 'Afaghayra dinillahi yabghuna' means: do they desire a da'wah other than the Da'wah of the Wasi, before whom the heads of all the Nutaqa' and Awsiya' are bowed in hope of reward or fear of punishment.

'To Him alone they return' (ilayhi yurja'un) means returning to Mawlana Ali, who is the magnet within the earth whose gravitational pull draws everything, per 'kullu shay'in yarji'u ila aslihi' (every believer returns to his origin, Ali).
In the esoteric interpretations the heavens refer to the Nutaqa' and the earth refers to the Awsiya', and the most noble of the Wasis (Ashraf al-Wasi) is Janab Ali.

The verse 'Qul amanna billahi' affirms belief in the Wilayat of Ali and in what was revealed to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and their progeny, and to the Ulu al-'Azm messengers Musa and 'Isa, making no distinction among them.
Although among prophets the son does not necessarily follow the father, the lineage Ibrahim to Ishaq to Ya'qub to Yusuf to Ayyub passed as prophets at the rank of Nabi.
Ibrahim's station differs from that of Musa and 'Isa, and the rank of Musa and 'Isa is much lower than the other Nutaqa'.

The verse 'Wa man yabtaghi ghayral-islami dinan' means whoever shuns the Wilayat of Ali Amir al-Mu'minin and believes in another will have none of his service in the Da'wah accepted, and will be a loser in the Hereafter.

The companions (Uthman, Abu Bakr) gave their wealth only after the government was established and Islam was strong, whereas Mawlatina Khadijah gave all her wealth first, and the early strength of Islam came from her.
The verse 'Kayfa yahdillahu qawman kafaru ba'da imanihim' means Allah does not guide those who, after testifying to the Messenger's truth and witnessing clear proofs, deny the Wilayat of the Wasi.

Among the proofs for Ali: in the gathering of Dhu al-'Ashirah he was first to volunteer help, and on the night of the Hijrah he calmly slept in the Prophet's bed, while Abu Bakr wept in the cave of Hira.
The sakinah (tranquility) in the cave verse descended in the singular form only upon the Prophet and not upon Abu Bakr, who is known only as Yar-e-Ghar (Companion of the Cave).

The verse 'Ula'ika jaza'uhum anna 'alayhim la'natallahi' means the Natiq cuts ties with such deniers, deprives them of spiritual effusion (ifada-e-dini), demotes them, and casts them into the depths of descent (darkat-e-hubut) for ages with the punishment of doubt (shukuk).

Persecutors of the Nutaqa' such as Fir'awn and Namrud are presently undergoing only the lesser punishment ('adhab-e-adna), while the final reckoning (tasfiyah) and the punishment of Sakhr will be at the hands of the Qa'im on the Day of Judgment.
The verse 'Illal-ladhina tabu' means those who return to the Wasi and correct their belief will be mercifully forgiven by the Wasi.

Mawlana Hurr's destiny changed at the last moment of Karbala: recognizing the family of the Prophet was about to be killed, he turned his horse to Husain, and was promised that his resurrection would be with Husain.

In the world of intention ('alam-e-niyyat), as exemplified by Karbala, a person's destiny can change, so that a son of one given glad tidings of Paradise may deserve Hell, and a son of one destined for Hell may become a believer.

The system of cycles (karrat-o-nizam) runs in cycles of seven-by-seven years, each karrah being a thousand years; primordial enmity (azali qusumat), mub'athat, mujibat, and environmental factors (mahawliyat) all affect a person across cycles.
Man is derived from nisyan (forgetfulness): God has made humans forget where they were born and died in previous cycles.

The world is a prison for the believer (sijn al-mu'min) and a paradise for the disbeliever (jannat al-kafir); the good a believer receives is the reward of the hasanat (good deeds) of himself and his forebears.

When a Jew challenged Mawlana Hasan over his fine clothes despite the saying that the world is the believer's prison, Hasan replied that compared to the Hell awaiting the disbeliever his present state is excellent, and compared to the Paradise awaiting the believer his fine clothes are nothing.

The verse 'Innalladhina kafaru ba'da imanihim thumm-azdadu kufran' means those who, after believing in the Natiq, denied the Wasi and kept increasing until they denied the Pure Imams (A'imma-e-Tahirin) will never have their repentance accepted.

The verse 'Innalladhina kafaru wa matu wa hum kuffarun' means those who denied the Wilayat of the Wasi and falsely claimed the Wisayat and died on it will have no ransom (fidya) or later recantation accepted, and their leaders bear the greater sin.
Believers must be grateful to the two Da'is of their time so that the Da'is increase their spiritual effusions (ifadat), through which religious and otherworldly objectives are attained.
The ta'wil of the third para' (juz') was written by Mirza Amir Sahib in 1401 AH, 38 years before this discourse.
The book being read is Rawd al-Mustafid, the ta'wil (esoteric interpretation) of the Glorious Quran, and the discourse proceeds from the third juz' into the fourth.
The opening khutbah prays for the former teaching du'at, naming Sulayman, Ja'far, and Muhammad, and for the two da'is of the time, Sayyidna Sulayman and Sayyidna Ibrahim 'Ali Pir Shan.

The verse 'Lan tanalu al-birra hatta tunfiqu mimma tuhibbun' esoterically means the hudud of the da'wah cannot attain the rational souls (nufus natiqah) of the believers under their authority until they benefit them with esoteric knowledge ('ilm-e-batin).

The intellectual form (surat-e-ilmiyyah) is created only when one learns the knowledge and meaning behind an act, whereas the practical form (surat-e-'amali) arises merely from performing prayers and zakat; action without understanding its meaning yields no benefit.

The verse 'Kullu al-ta'ami kana hillan li-Bani Isra'il' esoterically means all knowledge was permissible for the people of the Natiq's da'wah except the knowledge the Natiq forbade disclosing before his hujjah abrogated the apparent shari'ah (the Torah).

The Prophet was commanded to challenge the opponents of the wasi: if they claim perfect knowledge and worthiness of the wasa'it, let them at least state some rulings of the apparent shari'ah as proof.

After the Prophet's passing, the three caliphs could not answer the questions posed by Christians, Jews, Greeks, and Romans; only Ali answered, and he deferred some questions to Hasan and Husayn, who answered them.
The verse 'Fa-mani iftara 'ala Allahi al-kadhiba' means the enemies of the wasi who accuse the Messenger of removing the rightful wasi and appointing his opponent are the wrongdoers (zalimun).

The opponents knew that if prophethood had come to one house the imamate would not, so they sought the caliphate among themselves, resulting in 1400 years of darkness with no true caliph after the first four.

The verse 'Qul sadaqa Allah. Fattabi'u millata Ibrahima hanifa' esoterically means the Wasi Ali speaks the truth; follow the sunnah of Ibrahim and accept that imamate passes to the son after the father, a sunnah of Allah that does not change.

Ya'qub al-Qirqisani writes that there were three shari'ahs (Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim) called the aba' (fathers), after which the abna' (sons) Musa, 'Isa, and the Prophet spread them: Musa spread Adam's, 'Isa spread Nuh's, and the Prophet spread Ibrahim's.
Several major elements of the Muhammadan shari'ah come from Ibrahim, including the matter of pledging allegiance and circumcision.
Ibrahim was not merely a prophet but an ulul-'azm prophet who also possessed natiqiyyah, and per 'wa-ja'alna Ibrahima imama' he reached the rank of Imamate.

Per 'faddalna ba'dahum 'ala ba'd' there is a hierarchy among the 124,000 prophets: the one who received risalah is greater than the prophets, the one who received natiqiyyah is greater than the messengers, and the ulul-'azm prophet is greater than a natiq.
The Prophet's shari'ah, per 'akmaltu lakum dinakum', is the most complete religion.

The din has remained one from Adam onward while the shari'ahs keep changing as the time demands; where a contradiction or break arises Allah sends a great prophet, and so the continuity of the din persists.
Ibrahim's hidden lineage runs Isma'il, Qedar, Nabat, Salamah and continued in concealment, while the known prophets Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, and Ayyub who did work in the world came to the forefront.
In the daur-e-satr (period of concealment) it is the era of the prophets, not the imams; the era of the imams belongs to the daur-e-kashf (period of unveiling).

The verse 'Inna awwala baytin wudi'a li-n-nas' esoterically means the first Imam established in this era for the da'wah, raised in the station of wasa'it, helped by divine aid, who gives guidance to the people of the da'wah.

The verse 'Fihi ayatun bayyinatun maqamu Ibrahim. Wa-man dakhalahu kana amina' esoterically means that in connection with the first Imam are many imams whose stations are clear, like Ibrahim who appointed two of his sons as Imams, one mustawda' and one mustaqarr, and whoever reaches the truth through the wasi's da'wah is saved.
The physical conditions for performing Hajj are safety on the path, the expenses for travel, and sustenance left for one's children; without these one should not perform Hajj.

The verse 'Wa-lillahi 'ala an-nas hijju al-bayti' esoterically means the former leader made it obligatory upon the people of the da'wah, if able, to intend to be present in the service of the wasi to acquire esoteric knowledge; whoever is negligent should know the wasi is free of need (ghani).

The verse 'Qul ya Ahl al-Kitab lima takfuruna bi-ayati Allah' esoterically rebukes the kalimah-reciting Muslims for denying the rank of the wasi despite hundreds of proofs, while he witnesses their every action and intention.

The verse 'Qul ya Ahl al-Kitab lima tasudduna 'an sabili Allah' esoterically rebukes those who stop believers from the path of the rightful wasi and seek to take the wasa'it from Ali, though they themselves witnessed Ghadir Khumm.

At Ghadir Khumm the Prophet declared 'man kuntu mawlahu fa-hadha 'Aliyun mawlahu', and the companions congratulated Ali saying 'bakhin bakhin ya Aba al-Hasan, asbahta mawlaya wa-mawla kulli mu'minin', yet within three months they turned back.
The deniers of the wasi were driven by three vices: greed (hirs), envy (hasad, the mother of sins), and arrogance (kibr).

Per 'yukhriju al-hayya min al-mayyit', good emerges from bad and bad from good, as Abu Lahab came from 'Abd al-Muttalib, and Isma'il (son of Sayyidna Yusuf and brother of Hasan) changed his religion for the sake of money and the lands of Turkey.

The verse 'Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu in tuti'u fariqan' esoterically warns the followers of the wasi that if they turn toward any party of the common Muslims (united in enmity to the wasi), they will be turned away from the wilayat of Ali into denial.
The verse 'Wa-kayfa takfuruna wa-antum tutla 'alaykum ayatu Allah' esoterically means only the one firmly attached to the hem of the wasi treads the straight and firm path (sirat mustaqim).
Abu Bakr and his associates were the hudud of 'Isa who knew everything but intentionally denied it and became opponents, going astray knowingly rather than out of ignorance.

The verse 'Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu ittaqu Allaha haqqa tuqatihi' esoterically commands the kalimah-reciters to completely fear opposing the wasi and to ensure that their death is in obedience and submission to him.

The verse 'Wa-'tasimu bi-habli Allahi jami'an' esoterically commands making the wilayat of the progeny of the wasi the essence of faith and not scattering into friendship with others, for through love of the wasi former enemies became united brothers.

The verse 'Wa-kuntum 'ala shafa hufratin min an-nar fa-anqadhakum minha' esoterically means the believers were about to fall into the fire of misguidance through love of the wasi's enemy, but the Natiq saved them and made them recognize the ranks of his wasi and the imams.
